title: Jeremiah 20:1–6
context: Pashhur, son of Immer, a priest and chief officer in the temple, hears Jeremiah’s prophecy, strikes him, and puts him in the stocks. When released the next day, Jeremiah announces that the LORD has renamed Pashhur Magormissabib and that Pashhur and his household will go captive to Babylon. This Pashhur is identified by his father Immer and should not be assumed to be the Pashhur son of Malchijah of 21:1 and 38:1; how, if at all, these men were related is not stated.

verses.text: Now Pashhur, the son of Immer the priest, who was chief officer in the LORD’s house, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things.
verses.arminianNotes: Now Pashhur, the son of Immer the priest, who was chief officer in the LORD’s house, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things. Arminian readers see a religious leader choosing to silence God’s messenger rather than heed him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Immer was a priestly family (1 Chronicles 24:14). This Pashhur is distinguished by his father from the Pashhur son of Malchijah in 21:1 and 38:1; any relation between them is not stated.

verses.text: Then Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks that were in the upper gate of Benjamin, which was in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Then Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks that were in the upper gate of Benjamin, Arminian readers see the cost of faithfulness, as the prophet suffers public humiliation and pain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the stocks were in the LORD’s house itself, a bitter irony. The exact location of the upper gate of Benjamin is uncertain, though it was evidently near the temple.

verses.text: On the next day, Pashhur released Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then Jeremiah said to him, “The LORD has not called your name Pashhur, but Magormissabib.
verses.arminianNotes: On the next day, Pashhur released Jeremiah out of the stocks. Arminian readers see Jeremiah undaunted after a night of suffering, speaking the word he was given without softening it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah announces a new name for Pashhur, Magormissabib. The name is commonly connected with the theme of terror in 20:4 and 20:10, though its exact sense is discussed.

verses.text: For the LORD says, ‘Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They will fall by the sword of their enemies, and your eyes will see it. I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will carry them captive to Babylon, and will kill them with the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: For the LORD says, ‘Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. Arminian readers see Pashhur’s opposition to God’s word bringing on him the very fear he tried to suppress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this is the first time in the book that Babylon is named as the agent of judgment. The word against one man becomes a word about all Judah.

verses.text: Moreover I will give all the riches of this city, and all its gains, and all its precious things, yes, I will give all the treasures of the kings of Judah into the hand of their enemies. They will make them captives, take them, and carry them to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: Moreover I will give all the riches of this city, and all its gains, and all its precious things, Arminian readers see the treasures in which Jerusalem trusted surrendered to the enemy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the plundering of the city and royal treasures is later narrated in 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 52. The parallels can be named without merging their details.

verses.text: You, Pashhur, and all who dwell in your house will go into captivity. You will come to Babylon, and there you will die, and there you will be buried, you, and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: You, Pashhur, and all who dwell in your house will go into captivity. Arminian readers note that Pashhur is charged with having prophesied falsely, a priest who also spoke as a prophet of false hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the judgment on Pashhur is personal and complete: captivity, death, and burial in Babylon. His false assurance is answered by the true word he rejected.
